reply: Ask once, cheerfully, once you have picked the thing - "is there anything you can do on the price?" - then stop talking and be ready to walk away: silence and a customer who will leave are what move a price. Take the display model or last season's colour, offer to pay in full today, check the online price so they can match it, and never say your maximum. At a market or car boot sale, offer about two thirds and settle in the middle.
Sleep that won't come makes everything else twice as hard. Same getting-up time every day is the bit that steadies it.

Write down what comes in each month, then what goes out in two piles: the fixed ones (rent, bills, travel, debt) and the ones you decide week by week (food, going out, clothes). What is left is what you can save or throw at a debt, and if the piles add up to more than comes in, cut from the weekly ones first because that is where the slack is. The 50/30/20 shape - half on needs, a third on wants, a fifth on saving - is a starting point, not a rule, and a notes app you check every Sunday beats a clever spreadsheet you never open.

A dog is bored because the day is short on sniffing and chewing, not because he needs more toys. One walk where he is allowed to stop and sniff does more than a long march, and a scatter of his dinner on the lawn or in a snuffle mat takes ten minutes off the clock. Add five minutes of training a day, something legal to chew and a game of tug, and break the day up rather than saving it all for the evening.

Homework earns its place in small doses: about ten minutes a night in the first years of primary, half an hour by the end of it and an hour or so at secondary, and the evidence for it is weakest for the youngest children. What makes it work is the same each night - a fixed time, a clear table, and you nearby without taking over. If it is regularly taking much longer than the school's own limit, or ending in tears, that is worth one short message to the teacher rather than a battle every evening.

Start with very little: trainers or astro boots, shorts or leggings, a water bottle and, for football or hockey, shin pads. Clubs lend sticks, bats and bibs to beginners, so email and ask what they provide before you buy anything.

A modern screen is a grid of millions of pixels, each with red, green and blue lights under it, and the picture is just each one being told how bright to be for that frame. A new frame goes up 50 or 60 times a second, faster than your eye follows, which is what makes it look like smooth movement.

The Commons is the elected half of parliament: 650 MPs, one per constituency, and the party with a majority of those seats forms the government. MPs vote on the laws, question ministers - prime minister's questions is the Wednesday set-piece - and sit on select committees that go through a department's work line by line.

Maths and the sciences are learned by doing, not reading: work through the examples with the book open, then close it and do them again, then do past papers with the mark scheme next to you. Mark them honestly and write down the topics that lost marks; those get redone three days later. Learn the formulas by using them in questions rather than copying them out ten times, and if a topic still will not work, ask a teacher or a classmate to watch you do one question.

For a warm week: light cotton tops and shorts, one long-sleeved layer and a light waterproof, plus swimwear, a hat, high-factor sun cream and shoes you can walk in. Take two pairs of shoes at most and one smarter outfit if you plan to eat out; everything else can be washed.

Ask work first, then price the journey three ways before you buy anything: a season ticket only beats weekly or daily tickets above about three days a week, a flexi ticket or a carnet covers two or three days, and a railcard pays for itself in about a dozen trips if you qualify for one. If you drive, park and ride, a lift-share board or a parking space a ten-minute walk out usually undercuts the station car park, and asking whether your employer does a season ticket loan or a cycle-to-work scheme is free money in effect. Booking the next day's travel the night before is where the cheap fares go.

Half the fat to flour by weight: 250g plain flour and 125g cold butter rubbed in with a pinch of salt, then a few spoons of cold water to bring it together. Rest it in the fridge 30 minutes before rolling, and bake blind at 190C (170C fan) for 15 minutes for a flan case.

Use a virtual card: most banking apps make a one-off card number in a few taps, so the shop never holds the real details, and set a low limit on it. Where that is not offered, one card kept for online only, notifications on for every payment, and the real one frozen in the app between uses - most let you unfreeze it in seconds. Never save a card on a site you would not buy from twice, and check the last two digits and the merchant on any 'confirm this payment' prompt, because that is the step a scam tries to get you to tap through.

Under an hour you do not need to carry anything: have 300-500ml in the hour before you go and take water at fountains or taps on the way. Past an hour, or on a hot day, carry 400-700ml and drink a few mouthfuls every 15-20 minutes rather than one big stop. To keep it cold, fill the bottle half full and freeze it the night before, top it up with cold water on the way out, and put it in a belt or vest rather than in your hand. Over 90 minutes take electrolytes, and drink to thirst - drinking lots of plain water on a long run can make you feel worse, not better.

Under-fives usually travel free on local buses with a paying adult, and 5 to 15 pay a child fare, often about half: the operator's own page gives the age and the price for your area. Free travel to school is a council decision and it turns on distance - usually over 2 miles for a child under 8 and over 3 miles for an 8 to 16 year old going to the nearest suitable school, or closer if the route is unsafe to walk. Ask the council's school travel team; a 16 to 18 year old in full-time education usually needs a council or operator discount card instead.

A browser is the program you read websites in: Chrome, Safari, Edge and Firefox are the common four and they all do the same job. Anything you type in the address bar, any page you save a password for and any tab you leave open belongs to that one browser, which is why an account that works on your phone can look lost on a laptop until you sign in.

Anything that gets you warm and out of breath counts, so pick the kind you will actually turn up for three times a week: brisk walking, cycling, swimming, stairs, dancing or a run-walk. Add two short strength sessions - squats or sit-to-stands, press-ups on the stairs or against the worktop, a row with a band or a loaded bag - because muscle is what keeps carrying and climbing easy. Three half-hours and two strength sessions a week is plenty to start, and adding five minutes or one rep a week beats changing everything at once.

Motivation follows action, not the other way round: do ten minutes and decide after. Pick the subject you least dread but find easiest to start with, because a bad day is about getting one thing done, not all of it. If it has felt pointless for weeks, tell someone at school or work; that is a different problem from laziness.

A life cycle is the stages a living thing goes through from one generation to the next: a frog goes egg, tadpole, froglet, adult, and a butterfly goes egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly. A plant's is seed, seedling, flowering plant, then seed again. The adult stage is the one that makes the next generation, which is what closes the circle.

A waterproof with a hood is the one thing that decides the day, with a thin layer underneath rather than a thick coat, because rain gear is warm once you move. Wear shoes that keep water out - leather or a waterproof boot rather than canvas, which soaks and stays wet - and take a second pair of socks. Cotton next to the skin is what makes a wet day cold, so a synthetic or wool base layer is worth more than an extra jumper.

Learn four shapes first - G, C, D and E minor - because those four are most of the songs you already know, and practise moving between two of them rather than holding one well. Ten minutes a day: one minute of slow changes with a metronome or a steady count, then play a song with the same two chords in it, and add a third only when the change is clean.

The things that work: same wake-up time every day, no caffeine after early afternoon, not much alcohol in the evening (it wakes you in the second half of the night), a cool dark room, and getting out of bed if you're awake for more than 20 minutes. Screens off half an hour before bed and a short walk most days help more than any app. If you're worn out all day too, or it has gone on for weeks, ask a GP: they can check your bloods, and broken sleep plus no energy is worth ruling out.

Pick one thing for two weeks, not five: a twenty-minute walk after a meal, a vegetable with every main meal, or water instead of the second fizzy drink. Any one of those is most of what "healthier" means, one that sticks beats three that don't, and two weeks is long enough to know whether it fits your week. Which of the three could you start tomorrow?

Go at the time you would actually go, on a weekday evening if that is when you are free: a gym that is full at six is the one you stop using. Then check three things - the distance from home or work, because anything past fifteen minutes gets skipped, whether the classes you want are included in the price or cost extra, and the notice period on the contract, which is often a month and sometimes three. Ask for a day pass or a week trial before you sign, look at the changing rooms as well as the equipment, and work out the price per visit rather than per month: 40 a month is cheap at three visits a week and dear at one. The cheapest gym is the one you actually use.

Keep the book where you idle - beside the kettle, in your bag, by the bed - and read in the small gaps instead of waiting for a free evening. Quit a book at about 50 pages if it has not gripped you: forcing yourself to finish things you dislike is what stops the habit.

Roughly £10 to £15 covers a secret santa or a colleague, £20 to £30 a friend or a nephew, £30 to £60 a close friend or a sibling, and £50 to £100 a partner or a parent. Fix a total for the year before December and divide it per person, and agree a cap out loud with a group: the number is a budget line, not a measure of how much you like someone.

Attach it to something you already do every day - after the kettle boils, after you brush your teeth - because a new habit needs an old one to hang on. Make the first version almost too small to fail (one page, one glass, two minutes), keep it in the same place and time, and put a tick on a wall calendar: the streak is what carries it past the first fortnight, when the novelty has gone.

Brush for a few minutes a day, working the small knots out with your fingers before the brush touches them so it never pulls: a slicker brush for a short coat, an undercoat rake for a double coat. Do not shave a double coat, because it is his insulation in hot weather as well as cold. Ears and paws are the parts people forget, and anything that needs clippers is worth watching a groomer do once.

Most forgetting is not a lost file: new memories fade unless they are slept on and retrieved, and the brain clears out details to keep the gist; being tired, stressed or trying to hold too much at once makes it worse. Write things down and sleep on it; if you are forgetting recent conversations or the names of people you know well, get it checked.

Shoes are decided by length and width, so buy for the longer foot and the wider one - the two are rarely the same - and try them late in the day when your feet are at their biggest, in the socks or tights you will wear. A thumb's width at the toe, the widest part of the shoe at the widest part of your foot, and no lift at the heel when you walk: if the heel slips, a smaller size will pinch the toe instead. Leather gives a little, so a leather shoe should be snug rather than roomy, and a synthetic one will not give at all.

Cook two big things on one day and portion them: a pot of chilli or bolognese and a tray of roast veg, then cook rice or pasta fresh on the day. Cool it within two hours, box it in the portions you will actually eat, and keep three days in the fridge or freeze the rest. Chop an onion, wash a bag of salad and grate some cheese while you are there and a weekday dinner takes ten minutes. Cooked rice is the one to freeze on the day, not the next.

Start with two walks a week you could hold a conversation through, 20 minutes each, and add five minutes a week rather than a new plan: after years off, the first month is about the habit and the tendons, not the heart. Add two short strength sessions (sit to stand, a push, a pull) once the walking feels easy, and expect soreness for a day or two, not for a week. If you have a heart condition, joint trouble or are over 60 and have not exercised in years, a word with a GP first is sensible.

A short nap is worth having: 20 minutes, ideally before about 3pm, and set an alarm, because 90 minutes leaves you groggier than when you lay down. It helps most if you lost sleep the night before or you are driving later. Skip it if you already lie awake at night, and if you need one every afternoon for weeks, that is worth a word with the GP, especially with low mood, thirst or weight loss.

Earache in an adult is usually a cold or a sore throat spreading to the middle ear, and it settles in a few days: paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose on the pack, a warm flannel over it, and don't poke anything in. See a GP if it lasts more than three days, if there is discharge from the ear, or if you also have a high temperature or swelling behind the ear.

One room at a time, three bags on the floor — bin, donate, keep — and the donate bags go to the car the same day or they drift back. Ten minutes a day beats a lost weekend, and start with the room you walk through most, because clearing that one is what makes the rest of the house feel possible.

Start at about half of what you think you can manage and go every other day for the first two weeks - 20 minutes of walking or easy cycling is plenty, and the aim is to finish feeling you could have done more. Add about a tenth a week after that, and expect the second day to be sorer than the first, which is normal, while a joint that hurts is a stop. Give it six weeks before you judge it, because the habit and the tendons come back more slowly than the muscle.

Mostly it is the setup, not willpower: enough sleep, food, the phone in another room and one thing open at a time. Work in 25-minute blocks on a single task written down first, because choosing where to start is half the distraction, and stand up for the break. If your mind wanders when you read, take notes by hand and say the page back to yourself in one line at the end of it.

Most adult dogs need 30 minutes to an hour a day, and a working breed rather more. A puppy is the other way round: about five minutes of walking for every month of age, twice a day, so a four-month-old gets two twenty-minute walks and no long hikes or stair runs until the growth plates close at a year. Flat-faced breeds and older dogs need less and overheat easily, so go by the dog rather than the breed chart. Running or cycling with a dog is the same rule at speed: wait until he is a year old, start with a mile and add a little each week, keep it on soft ground, and skip it on warm days, because a dog on hot tarmac is burnt pads and heat stroke.

Vets disagree about it, so ask yours about your own dog.

For a lease, an employment contract or anything over a few thousand pounds, have someone who does this read it; a union checks an employment contract free, and Citizens Advice will look at most others.
